title: Serielizados Prizes: Hagai Levi’s ‘Etty’ and ‘Astonishing’ ‘Killing a Bear’ Win Big as ‘El Observatorio’ Bags the Mind the Gap Pitch Prize
full_text: Oct 25, 2026 3:38am PT Serielizados Prizes: Hagai Levi’s ‘Etty’ and ‘Astonishing’ ‘Killing a Bear’ Win Big as ‘El Observatorio’ Bags the Mind the Gap Pitch Prize By Annika Pham Plus Icon Annika Pham Latest ‘Father’s House,’ Starring David Dencik and Trine-Dyrholm, Picked Up by DR Sales Ahead of Tallinn Competition 4 days ago Tallinn Baltic Event: New Movie From Darko Lungulov and Ernestas Jankauskas, Plus Titles Directed by Rising Talents Josh Trigg, Marina Palacio and Many More 6 days ago Serielizados Program: Steven Moffat, Ferran Adrià and Rodrigo Sorogoyen Bring Star Creator Power to Barcelona 1 week ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Etty Courtesy of Arte France Influential Israeli creator Hagai Levi (“The Affair,” “Scenes From a Marriage”) and prominent Spanish TV-making duo Jorge and Alberto Sánchez-Cabezudo (“La Zona”) won best international and national series at Barcelona’s Serielizados for “Etty” and “Killing a Bear” respectively. The prizes for Serielizados two competitive sections were announced Saturday night at a Serielizados awards ceremony. Popular on Variety Related Stories Netflix, ‘Elite’ Star Ester Expósito and Locarno Winner Mar Coll Adapt ‘La Regenta,’ a ‘Fresh Female Perspective’ on a Big Spanish Classic (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Black Shine, From 'State of Silence' Director Santiago Maza, ’ Delves Into the Aftermath of a 2006 Mining Tragedy That Buried 63 Miners Both series in six-parts reflect the boldness of their respective creators, who broke new ground within traditional genres. In the French-Dutch-German show “ Etty ,” based on Dutch Jewish author Etty Hillesum’s diaries, Levi deliberately opted for a modern spin to the period piece in which we follow the passionate 27-year-old Etty as she embarks on a spiritual and emotional journey in a Nazi-occupied Amsterdam. In the Spanish show “ Killing a Bear ” (“Matar a un oso”) the Sánchez-Cabezudo brothers brought innovation to the crime genre, making a bear the victim, relating the crime from the POV of multiple characters, and expanding the number of prime suspects to a tight community of 262 Anti-Bears chat room in Spain’s idyllic high-Pyrenean Val d’Arán. “With this series, we felt really lucky to have been invited into a world so fully realised, so distinctly Catalan but portrayed with a confidence and a muscularity that left us astonished,” said Finnish producer Roosa Toivonen, also Tallinn TV Beats co-head, who sat on the national competition jury with Canneseries’ Claire-Marine Pietriga and the Berlinale’s Rowan Woods. ‘Kiling a Bear’ Both series also stand out among the best shows that Europe currently has to offer, with the stamp of approval from quality-maker Arte France . Indeed, the European cultural channel was a major backer of Levi’s historical drama – conceived as a feature film in six episodes – which world-premiered out of competition in Venice, was highlighted at Series Mania, and bowed in French cinemas May 6 before launching on Arte.tv on May 16. Shepherded by Les Films du Poisson, “Etty” is sold internationally by Studio TF1 . “Killing a Bear” which had its Catalan premiered at Serielizados fast on the heels of its world premiere at Spain’s Valladolid Film Festival, is the latest prime example of Arte France’s successful collaboration with the largest Spanish pay-TV/SVOD operator Movistar Plus. The Movistar Plus Original, produced by the Sánchez-Cabezudo brothers’ Studio TF1-owned Kubik Films, will bow in Spain Dec. 1. Besides the top win for “Etty,” Arte France also scooped best screenplay at Serielizados’ official International Selection Awards for the French comedy “Camarades” co-created and co-penned by Benjamin Charbit (“Under Control”) and Dominique Baumart (“The Bureau”). Another comedy wooed the international jury: BBC’s hit show “Ann Droid” for which its creator, Bafta-nominated Diane Morgan (“Mandy,” “Cun”), won best performance for her turn as the second-hand robot Linda. On the national competition front, all four selected series won accolades. Next to “Killing a Bear,” the anticipated drama “Segunda Temporada” from the hot creators of Filmin’s “Autodefensa” – writer-director Miguel Ángel Blanca and co-writers Berta Prieto and Víctor Diago – scooped best screenplay. Bringing together a washed-up ghost-writer and a fading trap legend fresh out of jail, the show was developed as part of Serielizados Kick talent lab, before making it as a 7-30-minute drama produced by Barcelona-based Boogaloo Films and Canada. Paris-based Oble handles sales. Beloved Spanish-acting queen Carmen Machi (“Aida,” “La Mesías”), bagged a fresh best actress nod for her performance as tax inspector Sara Santano in the Movistar Plus-100 Balas’ “Celeste” Season 2 which bowed as a world premiere in Barcelona. Last year the show’s creator Diego San José and helmer Elena Trapé scooped two Serielizados wins for “Yakarta,” another example of their inimitable downbeat but sharply observant humor. Elsewhere, the buzzy HBO Max-3Cat co-commissioned dramedy “In Vitro” which offers a witty and heart-warming look at fertility treatments, received a Special Mention. “This [show] really stood out to us for its global appeal and international remake potential,” said the jurors. The series, created by Marc Crehuet with Alejandra Guimerà, was co-penned by Crehuet with Carmen Marfá, Natalia Boadas and Serielizados co-founder Víctor Sala. The latter said the show ,which launched simultaneously Oct. 19 in Spain on HBO Max and 3Cat, garnered an excellent 18.2% share on the Catalan pubcaster. “Many countries could be jealous of the creative courage the Spanish commissioners have shown, as they have helped equally bold producers to greenlight shows of this caliber!” said the jurors of the Spanish competition, who highlighted the central female-characters of different ages in each of the four series. The jurors added: “Serializados is one of these tremendous gems – smaller events where you can see that the content is lovingly hand-picked and curated out of pure passion for the art and craft of series, and the atmosphere is convivial with a lovely team that truly cares about everyone’s experience and hospitality. We, the jury members, had a great time and watching the four nominated shows was a lot of fun, as they are each so brilliant and original in their very unique ways.” Although Serielizados has another few days to run – until Oct. 28 – across various Barcelona venues, co-founder and festival programmer Betu Martínez Molero was pleased with this 13 th edition, led by masterclasses with Levi, Steven Moffat and Sue Vertue, a full day of the Miniput -quality TV festival showcase, and the second edition of the Mind the Gap pitch competition. Mind the Gap The top €5,500 ($6,100) Mind the Gap Award was handed out to the creators of the Spanish show “El Observatorio,” from Laura Roqué, Luis Sorolla and Eloy Zamora. Set in a small village from Sierra Morena, the story turns on a group of astrophysicists investigating mysterious flickering lights, until one of them-Sara starts to believe the light might be her deceased father trying to communicate. “After a great deliberation we’ve decided to award new talent who need to be discovered,” said Arte France’s Alexios Kastrissianakis, co-juror with Mubi’s Ben Driscoll, Movistar Plus’ Laura Escrivá, ZDF Studios’ Susanne Frank and Beta Film’s Peter Lohner. First pitched at the ECAM Forum 2026 where it earned the Serilizados award, the project, in early development, is looking for a producer. The jury also gave two honorable mentions to two female-led series about abuse: the Finnish psychological drama “Dangerous Woman,” produced by Gutsy Pictures for MTV Finland and TV4 Sweden, and the Spanish drama “Callback” created by sisters Joana and Mireia Vilapuig for “This is Not Sweden” producer Funicular Films, with Left Tackle Films. “Callback” was also bestowed the €2,000 ($2,200) Konga Music Agency award. Martínez Molero said: “This year we solidified our position as the leading international TV series festival in Spain and one of the most prominent in Southern Europe, reaching 18.000 attendees across more than 60 activities, including more than 30 national and international premieres.” He added: “We’ve seen a growing interest from both media and audiences for our National and International Competitions, packing our main venues. It’s also been great to see how presenting non-distributed international shows helps put them on the radar of Spanish platforms looking to acquire new series, while also helping local creators connect with key international players in the TV industry.” Following its onsite showcase in Barcelona, Serielizados will bow on line on the streamer Filmin over Nov. 10-22. title: Egyptian Cinema Eyes Its Next Act as Industry Veterans Call for Better Scripts, Wider Distribution
full_text: Oct 25, 2026 2:16am PT Egyptian Cinema Eyes Its Next Act as Industry Veterans Call for Better Scripts, Wider Distribution By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest El Gouna Takeaways: ‘Safe Exit’ Wins Top Prize, Arab TV Seeks New Talent and Egyptian Filmmakers Push Boundaries 1 day ago El Gouna’s CineGouna Expands Industry Push: ‘We Want to Give Every Filmmaker a Chance’ 2 days ago British Filmmaker Joanna Hogg on the Fight to Turn Personal Stories Into Fiction: ‘Each Time I’m Learning From Scratch’ 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Mohamed Mashish, Hadi El Bagoury, Ziad Srouji (Courtesy of Abdallah Sabry, Mohamed Osama, Ziad Srouji) As the ninth edition of El Gouna Film Festival wrapped in Egypt , the conversation among some of the country’s and region’s leading producers and filmmakers turned to what the industry needs to turn its wealth of talent into films that can find audiences both at home and abroad. Egyptian cinema once dominated film production across the Arab world, but output fell dramatically from its late-20th-century heights. According to figures from the Egyptian Chamber of Cinema Industry, the country produced 112 films in 1988, before output fell to just 16 a decade later. More recently, production has shown signs of recovery, rising from 51 feature films in 2022 to 67 in 2023. Related Stories ‘Industry,’ ‘Doctor Who’ Producer Jane Tranter on Resisting Trends, Centering Women and Telling Stories About ‘People Being Accepted for Who They Choose to Be’ Netflix Joins New Edition of Santiago-Guadalajara Queer Incubator For veteran Syrian producer Mohamed Mashish , who has built a decades-long career in Egypt, capitalizing on that momentum starts with the screenplay. Popular on Variety “We need to have more time for development and scriptwriting,” he tells Variety . “We have all the industry components. But we don’t have scripts. So what can you do? I have a nice camera, a good DP, but we can’t do anything without good scripts.” Mashish has seen firsthand how new platforms can expand the reach of Egyptian storytelling. He produced the 2016 drama “Grand Hotel,” which became the first Egyptian and first Arabic-language series to land on Netflix when the streamer released it internationally as “Secret of the Nile” in 2018. He believes younger filmmakers are also benefiting from greater access to work from around the world. “They’re more open-minded. They’re connected on the internet and everything,” he notes. “Because the platforms are available now, they’re watching more than just our culture. So they are more open and they are ready to move.” But Mashish argues that new perspectives need to be matched with experience. “We have to bring the old generation and the new generation together,” he explains. “The new generation brings a different perspective, but cinema still needs experience, so we need to combine that new talent with the expertise that already exists in the industry.” Egyptian director Hadi El Bagoury , whose 2016 “Hepta: The Last Lecture” became the highest-grossing romantic film in Egyptian cinema, points to streaming as one of the biggest opportunities for homegrown talent. The growth of platforms, he argues, has given filmmakers more places to show their work while exposing audiences to a wider range of filmmaking. “You discover new stories, new directors, new genres,” he says. “You discover a lot more directors, DPs, actors and different styles.” That exposure is also changing what audiences expect from Egyptian cinema. “They want new genres, they want original stories,” El Bagoury says. The shift has particular consequences in the Gulf, a crucial market for Egyptian films. Mashish points to Saudi Arabia’s theatrical expansion as an example of how quickly audiences have evolved. “At the beginning, when the Saudis started to open cinemas, they accepted everything because it was new,” he recalls. “It’s like, ‘I will go to the cinema, I will have popcorn, no matter the kind of movie I will watch.'” “They are more selective than before,” he continues. “They will not accept just anything coming anymore. Because cinemas are now open in Saudi and in the Gulf, they are watching international cinema. So they demand this kind of quality.” For Lebanese producer and distributor Ziad Srouji (“ Palestine 36 ”), whose career spans film and television across the Arab world, reaching audiences beyond the region does not mean making Arab films resemble foreign ones. “Specificity travels; generic does not,” he stresses. “International buyers aren’t looking for Arab films that imitate Western genre cinema, and they’re tired of films made only to explain the region to outsiders. They want stories rooted in a very particular world but driven by a premise anyone can grasp in one sentence.” For Srouji, the challenges often come after the initial idea. “A good idea gets you into the room. It doesn’t get you through production, and it certainly doesn’t get you to an audience.” The bigger obstacles, he believes, are often structural. “Too many films reach the market without a sales agent attached early, without delivery materials ready and without a positioning strategy beyond a festival premiere,” Srouji says. “Sales and distribution need a strategy built from day one, not after the premiere.” El Gouna is among the regional festivals trying to strengthen the path from development onward. CineGouna, its industry arm, launched the Egyptian Voices strand this year, selecting four Egyptian projects in development for tailored training in pitching, packaging and co-production. El Bagoury argues that the industry also needs more ways to reach audiences directly. “We need more Egyptian-owned platforms, more theaters. Theaters that are cheap, accessible to all,” he says. “We need a lot of this so we don’t have to depend on anybody else. We need to show our films in our cinemas and on our platforms.” For Srouji, the ultimate measure of a healthy industry is not simply whether a filmmaker gets a movie made or lands a prestigious festival selection, but whether that success makes the next film possible. “A major festival selection is a launch, not a career,” he says. “Sustainable success is when your second film is easier to finance than your first.” ‘Decision to Leave’ Cinematographer Kim Ji-yong on Chasing Natural Light for Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’: ‘This Is the One Where We Worried, Debated and Planned the Most’ Netflix Sets Release Date for Rob Lowe Documentary ‘The Outsider’ South Asian Filmmakers to Vie for $150,000 at Tasveer Film Market as Netflix, Aamir Khan Pictures Attend Netflix’s ‘The Blue Road’ Director Han Jun-hee on Why Playing It Safe Is the Real Risk Italian Content Investment Dropped 7.4% in 2025 Largely Due to Uncertainty Over Domestic Tax Credits, Rome MIA Market Report Says ‘Under Siege,’ Netflix’s Second Most Ambitious Colombian Series – a ‘Huge Undertaking Even by Our Standards’ – Bows Nov. 6 Loading comments...

title: Jay-Z Brings His ‘Jay-Z 30’ Concert Series to a Close in Los Angeles With Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg and Too Short
full_text: Oct 25, 2026 1:42am PT Jay-Z Brings His ‘Jay-Z 30’ Concert Series to a Close in Los Angeles With Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg and Too Short By Steven J. Horowitz Plus Icon Steven J. Horowitz Senior Music Writer speriod Latest Jay-Z Brings His ‘Jay-Z 30’ Concert Series to a Close in Los Angeles With Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg and Too Short 5 hours ago Slayyyter Cancels Remaining European and U.K. Tour Dates to Recover From Laryngitis 2 days ago Former Eminem Employee Pleads Guilty to Stealing and Selling Unreleased Music 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Roc Nation How does one measure their own legacy: In a series of shows, in the decades since a debut album, in an exhaustive eight-part docuseries breaking down the intricacies of rhymes laid down years ago? That seemed to be the existential question looming over “ Jay-Z 30,” a yearlong celebration that began with a spectacular one-off headlining performance at the Roots Picnic in late May and concluded on Saturday night with the second of two shows at Inglewood, California’s SoFi Stadium. Related Stories Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’ Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s ‘Jengira’s Magnificent Dream,’ With Tilda Swinton, Boarded by ‘Triangle of Sadness’ Mexican Co-Producer Piano For Jay, legacy has clearly been weighing on his mind. A new generation of hip-hop artists has emerged, and the decade-long gap since he released an album has opened a space for that generation to question his legacy. So it made sense that he’d revisit his catalog brick by brick, show by show, celebrating a career-long work in progress that crescendoed to a global tour after nearly a decade of artistic dormancy. At SoFi, much like his previous concerts, his performance was a reminder — no, a reinforcement — that nothing at that scale is by accident. And he said as much as the curtain fell on an hour-and-a-half finale of his “Jay-Z 30” series, encouraging those in attendance to believe in what they’ve actually witnessed. Popular on Variety “You gotta be really real with what’s going on in the world,” he said during closer “Encore.” It was a direct rebuttal to the rash of tweets and social media posts claiming that SoFi wasn’t entirely sold out, or that many of the tickets had been given away. “People will tell you that nobody was in here tonight, but you got eyes. You can see. People will tell you that the music wasn’t great, but you got ears. You gotta understand, you gotta question everything. This world with AI and everything, it’s been going on forever. They called it propaganda before. But now, the technology has caught up and people are tricked. A lot of tricknology for us… Make sure you question everything you feel.” Jay-Z brings out Snoop Dogg and Dr. Dre for a medley of classics including “Nuthin’ But a G Thang” at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium pic.twitter.com/UGcAN433xi — Variety (@Variety) October 25, 2026 Jay makes that music that you can feel . That’s been the thrill of his shows over the past five months. For those who experienced his rise in real time (and, frankly, many at SoFi probably had, based on their millennial look), Jay has been a pop impresario, a cultural touchstone who helped graft hip-hop culture onto the mainstream. He’s done it through a breathless string of number one albums and hits, and in boardrooms and closed-door meetings. “Jay-Z 30” was an invitation to revisit the path that he took to get there, a way to show that legacy isn’t about the hit that’s next, but rather the ones you landed to get there. To witness it was where the details mattered most. Much like his other performances, the setlist at Jay’s final night at SoFi was somewhat static — “Girls, Girls, Girls,” for instance, once again bled into “’03 Bonnie & Clyde,” while “N—s in Paris” delightfully mashed into “Big Pimpin’.” But the finer details are what make a Jay show such an experience. At each of his shows, he’s found a way to pay homage to the city that’s welcomed him. In Philadelphia, that included guest appearances from Jazmine Sullivan, Bilal and his Roc-A-Fella crew, including Freeway, Beanie Sigel and Peedi Crakk. In New York City, throughout his three-night run at Yankee Stadium , he brought out Alicia Keys for “Empire State of Mind,” as well as Fat Joe and Jadakiss. Naturally, a narrative emerged: Can he really perform a solid headlining set without a supporting cast to sweeten the deal? Perhaps that’s why the guest count at his SoFi shows was so thin compared to others. On Saturday night, he tapped Too Short to perform “Blow the Whistle,” shouting out the Bay Area. Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg came out to do a medley of their own massive hits, including “Nuthin’ But a ‘G’ Thang” and “Still D.R.E.” But it was mainly Jay, every day , in all his resplendence. He traipsed from era to era, hit to hit, his breath control and spark as refined as ever. This was performance at its peak, a marvel to behold of an artist who helped build hip-hop as an institution while adding to the story still being written. Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg performing “Still D.R.E.” during Jay-Z’s final night at Inglewood’s SoFi Stadium pic.twitter.com/5VayWQblwJ — Variety (@Variety) October 25, 2026 As for what’s next? Rumors have swirled about a new album from collaborators who quickly backpedaled on their statements. The looming question mark of a Super Bowl Halftime Show performance hung in the air at SoFi on Saturday night. But for a string of concerts and a few activations here and there, it felt only right that Jay-Z justify the experience while rapping “Heart of the City (Ain’t No Love)” near the end of the show: “Jigga held you down 30 summers, damn, where’s the love?” Check out the full setlist below: The Watcher 2 Blow the Whistle (Too $hort) Izzo (H.O.V.A.) title: Soccer Drama ‘Forza,’ With AC Milan Great Alessandro Costacurta, Heads to Tokyo Market With EST N8 (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Oct 24, 2026 8:32pm PT Soccer Drama ‘Forza,’ With AC Milan Great Alessandro Costacurta, Heads to Tokyo Market With EST N8 (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Soccer Drama ‘Forza,’ With AC Milan Great Alessandro Costacurta, Heads to Tokyo Market With EST N8 (EXCLUSIVE) 9 hours ago ‘KPop Demon Hunters,’ ‘Squid Game’ Stars Fete Netflix’s Korea Decade as Ted Sarandos Teases ‘Tantara,’ ‘All of Us Are Dead’ Season 2 10 hours ago AI Firm Behind India’s ‘Mahabharat’ Series Turns to Indonesian Myth in Cross-Border IP Pact (EXCLUSIVE) 11 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Riva Studios “ Forza ,” Marco Balsamo’s soccer drama shot between Bali and Milan, has been picked up for international sales by EST N8 , which will take the film to the Tokyo International Film Festival ‘s TIFFCOM market (Oct. 28–30). Before that, it gets its first public screening on Oct. 25 at Jakarta Film Week. Balsamo’s first feature as director centers on Bima, an 11-year-old from Bali who hopes a career as a pro footballer will give his family a better life. A chance bond with a former AC Milan player in the last stretch of his career changes the outlook for both of them. Related Stories 50 Cent Opens Up About Diddy’s Secret Smear Campaign Against Him, Why He Won’t Work With Courtney Kemp Again and Learning His Mom Was Gay: ‘I’m Not Ashamed of That in Any Way’ Ryan Gosling’s Zero-G Stunts on ‘Project Hail Mary’ Broken Down by the Space Epic’s VFX Supervisors Newcomer Ghazi Alhabsyi heads the cast. Balsamo also appears on screen, alongside Tara Sibel Demren, AC Milan icon Alessandro Costacurta and Atiqah Hasiholan, Oka Antara and Tio Pakusadewo, all three winners at the Indonesian Film Festival (FFI). Popular on Variety Balsamo wrote the script and produced with Demren. Riva Studios originated the project, and its producers include Ario Sagantoro of “The Raid” franchise. Adhya Pictures has the film’s Indonesian theatrical release, set for 2027. Interest at home is strong. Both rounds of online tickets for the Jakarta screening, at CGV Grand Indonesia, sold out inside five minutes. “‘Forza’ follows a boy from Bali and a former pro footballer who open new doors for each other, and it bridges Indonesia and Italy the way only football can,” said Sophie Shi, head of studios at EST N8. “It’s a film for audiences around the world, with a story of family and hope that transcends language and culture. Our mission is to take bold Asian stories to audiences worldwide, and a family film told through the world’s most popular sport is built to travel. We’re proud to launch ‘Forza’ to buyers at TIFFCOM.” Shi and Jan Paul Villanueva negotiated the deal for EST N8, with Balsamo and Demren representing Riva Studios. Villanueva, EVP of acquisitions and global distribution, will lead sales with Cathy Ni, head of sales and U.S. distribution, and Shams Pasha, global sales and marketing executive. “We’ve spent years bringing ‘Forza’ to the screen, and Indonesia has been at the heart of it from the beginning,” Balsamo said. “This film is a labor of love and a testament to the perseverance and collaboration behind independent filmmaking. Sharing the film at Jakarta Film Week is especially meaningful. It’s a moment we’ve been looking forward to for a long time.” Demren, who co-founded Riva Studios, said the film was designed for families to watch side by side and discuss afterward. “We hope Bima’s journey reminds audiences how much it matters to have someone believe in you, especially when your dreams feel out of reach,” she said. “Seeing both ticket releases fill so quickly is an encouraging start. We’re looking forward to hearing audiences’ reactions.” Demren and Balsamo set up Riva Studios in 2022 as an independent outfit working in live action, animation and music. In 2024 it bought French animation house TeamTO. “Forza” is its first live-action feature. Also on EST N8’s TIFFCOM lineup are “Tame,” a Thai horror title from B-EST Pictures; Dean Colin Marcial’s crime thriller “Jaguar,” set in Manila; “Master,” Rezwan Shahriar Sumit’s winner of IFFR’s Big Screen Award; “Pilgrims,” a Korean sci-fi animation from Heo Pyoungkang that was selected for Annecy; and “The Invisible Half,” a J-horror from Nishiyama Masaki. The company, which brought together EST Studios and N8, has offices in Los Angeles and Bangkok and has sold and distributed more than 60 titles across over 100 territories. Its catalog includes “Hidden Letters,” which was shortlisted for the Oscars and nominated for an Emmy; “The Monk and the Gun,” Bhutan’s Oscar entry; “A Useful Ghost,” which won the Grand Prize at Cannes Critics’ Week; and “Blood Brothers,” which topped Netflix’s global chart. ‘Hatchet’ Movie: Netflix and Derek Cianfrance to Adapt Gary Paulsen’s Survival Book (EXCLUSIVE) Sex, Love and War: How the Racy Gay Epic ‘La Bola Negra’ Could Win Netflix’s First Best Picture Oscar Netflix Film VP Doug Belgrad Is Out Amid Layoffs CAA’s Roeg Sutherland Says It’s Too Soon to Predict Fallout From Netflix Firings, Thinks Recent Mergers Represent ‘Opportunity’ for Industry Netflix Sets Release Date for Rob Lowe Documentary ‘The Outsider’ ‘Decision to Leave’ Cinematographer Kim Ji-yong on Chasing Natural Light for Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’: ‘This Is the One Where We Worried, Debated and Planned the Most’ Loading comments...

title: ‘KPop Demon Hunters,’ ‘Squid Game’ Stars Fete Netflix’s Korea Decade as Ted Sarandos Teases ‘Tantara,’ ‘All of Us Are Dead’ Season 2
full_text: Oct 24, 2026 8:21pm PT ‘KPop Demon Hunters,’ ‘Squid Game’ Stars Fete Netflix’s Korea Decade as Ted Sarandos Teases ‘Tantara,’ ‘All of Us Are Dead’ Season 2 By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Soccer Drama ‘Forza,’ With AC Milan Great Alessandro Costacurta, Heads to Tokyo Market With EST N8 (EXCLUSIVE) 9 hours ago ‘KPop Demon Hunters,’ ‘Squid Game’ Stars Fete Netflix’s Korea Decade as Ted Sarandos Teases ‘Tantara,’ ‘All of Us Are Dead’ Season 2 10 hours ago AI Firm Behind India’s ‘Mahabharat’ Series Turns to Indonesian Myth in Cross-Border IP Pact (EXCLUSIVE) 11 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Netflix Stars of “ Squid Game ” and “ KPop Demon Hunters ” took the stage in Seoul on Oct. 24 as Netflix celebrated 10 years in Korea with a fan festival, where co-CEO Ted Sarandos previewed upcoming titles including “Tantara” and “All of Us Are Dead” Season 2. “Squid Game” was represented by Lee Jung-jae, Lee Byung-hun and Park Hae-soo, while Ahn Hyo-seop appeared for “KPop Demon Hunters.” Also on stage were Koo Kyo-hwan and Jung Hae-in of “D.P.,” Kim Hyun-joo of “Hellbound,” Yum Hye-ran of “Mask Girl” and Lee Se-dol of “The Devil’s Plan,” among others. Thousands of fans turned out for themed booths, games, merchandise and live music. Popular on Variety “Ten years ago, we dreamed big. But none of us could have imagined that Korean stories would move hearts around the world, and land right at the center of global culture,” Sarandos said. Of the new titles, Lee Chang-dong’s Venice winner “Possible Love,” headlined by Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Cho Yeo-jeong and Jo In-sung, bows Nov. 6. “Tantara,” starring Song Hye-kyo, Gong Yoo and Kim Seol-hyun, follows on Dec. 11. Still undated are “Grand Galaxy Hotel,” with Lee Do-hyun and Shin Si-a; “She, Wolf,” previously known by the working title “Beauty in the Beast,” with Kim Min-ju, Lomon and Moon Sang-min; “All of Us Are Dead” Season 2, with Park Ji-hu, Yoon Chan-young, Cho Yi-hyun and Lomon; and “Solo Leveling,” with Byeon Woo-seok. Netflix launched in Korea on Jan. 6, 2016. Its first international film was Bong Joon Ho’s “Okja.” The first Korean original, the stand-up special “Yoo Byung Jae: Too Much Information,” arrived in March 2018, and “Kingdom” became its first Korean series in January 2019. In July 2021, “Kingdom: Ashin of the North” became the first Korean show to crack the Global Top 10, charting in 58 countries. Netflix has counted upward of 200 Korean titles on its Global Top 10 since it began compiling the chart in June 2021. “Squid Game” Season 1 holds the record for the longest run at 32 straight weeks, nine of them at No. 1. The show’s three seasons are the streamer’s three most-watched non-English series ever, and “Teach You a Lesson” now ranks No. 10 on that list, making it Netflix’s biggest Korean show after “Squid Game.” No other non-English content draws more viewing on Netflix than K-content, and over four in five of its subscribers worldwide have sampled at least one Korean title. “For Netflix, Korea is more than a market. It is where we discovered new possibilities, and where we learned how far a story can travel. And it is one of our most treasured partners for the future we are building together,” Sarandos said. Between 2024 and 2026, first-time directors or writers made more than a third of Netflix’s Korean titles. Park Yoon-seo, an assistant director on “Kingdom” Season 2, made his directing debut this year with YA horror series “If Wishes Could Kill.” “Netflix gave me an opportunity when I was an assistant director on ‘Kingdom: Season 2.’ I’m glad I was able to give new actors that same opportunity,” Park said. He added that he had suggested casting only newcomers to keep the series fresh, and that Netflix signed off because fame wasn’t the priority. Baek Seung-min was a second lighting assistant on “Kingdom” and now heads lighting on “All of Us Are Dead” Season 2. “Working with Netflix Korea at important stages of my career has helped me grow professionally,” he said. From 2016 to 2025, Netflix partnered with more than 80 Korean production companies on shows employing upward of 20,000 actors and crew members, along with 70,000 extras and day workers. Shoots took place in more than 100 cities and towns, with over half outside the Seoul Capital Area in locations such as Busan, Jeonju and Jeju. “When Life Gives You Tangerines” alone drew on nearly 4,000 suppliers and a cast and crew of 600, adding more than KRW90 billion ($60.4 million) to the Korean economy. Netflix’s skills and training programs reached over 6,500 people in Korea between 2021 and 2025. To get those shows to viewers abroad, Netflix now relies on 122 localization partners globally, 119 of them dubbing studios. Colorist Park Jin-young, whose credits include “Possible Love” and “Good News,” said Netflix’s arrival in Korea came just as HDR technology was going commercial. “It felt like going from working with 30 colors of paint for 10 or 20 years to suddenly having 100 colors at my disposal,” he said. Unscripted formats have also exported well. “Physical: 100” became the first unscripted show not in English to lead the Global Top 10, and local versions have followed in Italy and Mexico, with U.S., French and Swedish editions on the way. The streamer also pointed to effects off screen. According to Netflix, 72% of subscribers who watch K-content have said they’d like to travel to Korea. Jeju drew about 2.24 million overseas visitors in 2025, its most in nine years, coinciding with the premiere of “When Life Gives You Tangerines,” while visits to the show’s Gimnyeong Beach location jumped about 96%. Chef Choi Hyun-seok’s restaurant Choi saw sales rise 300% after “Culinary Class Wars” Season 1, and bookings at restaurants of Season 2 contestants climbed 303%. In the U.S., new Korean learners on Duolingo rose 37% in the week “Squid Game” Season 3 launched. Applications for Korea’s TOPIK language exam passed 550,000 in September 2025, three months on from “KPop Demon Hunters,” beating the total for all of 2024. Between April 2025 and March 2026, K-content logged more than 12 billion viewing hours on Netflix, behind only U.S. productions, and rights to the “Hellbound” webtoon have sold to 11 countries since the series launched. Netflix has also opened a Korean-language microsite charting the people, locations and numbers behind its first decade in the country. title: AI Firm Behind India’s ‘Mahabharat’ Series Turns to Indonesian Myth in Cross-Border IP Pact (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Oct 24, 2026 7:30pm PT AI Firm Behind India’s ‘Mahabharat’ Series Turns to Indonesian Myth in Cross-Border IP Pact (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Soccer Drama ‘Forza,’ With AC Milan Great Alessandro Costacurta, Heads to Tokyo Market With EST N8 (EXCLUSIVE) 10 hours ago ‘KPop Demon Hunters,’ ‘Squid Game’ Stars Fete Netflix’s Korea Decade as Ted Sarandos Teases ‘Tantara,’ ‘All of Us Are Dead’ Season 2 10 hours ago AI Firm Behind India’s ‘Mahabharat’ Series Turns to Indonesian Myth in Cross-Border IP Pact (EXCLUSIVE) 11 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Collective Studios The AI technology behind Star Plus and JioHotstar series “ Mahabharat: Ek Dharmayudh ” is headed to Indonesia . There, its developer Galleri5 and fellow Collective company Collective Studios’ Historyverse plan to create film and series properties drawn from the country’s myths and history. Historyverse, which handles original IP and studio work for Collective Artists Network , is partnering with Galleri5 and Singhasari Special Economic Zone on the venture. Projects will cover mythology, fantasy, history and animation. Indonesian creatives and cultural specialists will work alongside Historyverse’s IP development team, using production tools Galleri5 built in India. Related Stories Ryan Gosling’s Zero-G Stunts on ‘Project Hail Mary’ Broken Down by the Space Epic’s VFX Supervisors How 'Whalefall' Production Designer Ramsey Avery Built the Creature's Stomach Using Mattress Foam and Silicone Bits The first project being discussed is “Echoes of Nusantara,” a working title for an original mythology-adventure. Historyverse will run creative development, production and IP packaging, and will collaborate with local talent to get projects ready for possible financing, production and distribution outside Indonesia. Popular on Variety “The next global entertainment franchises will not all come from Hollywood,” said Vijay Subramaniam, founder and group CEO of Collective Artists Network. “Every market has stories that deserve to travel further, and Indonesia has an extraordinary wealth of them. Our ambition with Collective Studios’ Historyverse is to work with Indonesian creators to develop these stories into films, series and larger entertainment properties for the world. Galleri5 gives us a new way to approach the scale of filmmaking, while the creative vision and the stories themselves remain at the center.” Galleri5’s main product, G5 AI Studio, brings more than 200 AI models together with purpose-built tools for storyboarding, designing characters and worlds, animation, VFX and film-quality video. More than 10,000 ads and videos have been made on the platform. JioStar and Collective Media Network launched “Mahabharat: Ek Dharmayudh,” and Galleri5 built and ran the AI filmmaking technology behind the show. The company is now developing workflows for Historyverse’s theatrical slate, which includes “Chiranjeevi Hanuman – The Eternal” and “Krishna.” Those productions give Galleri5 a base for refining its technology against real-world creative and production demands. “The next generation of global cinema will be built on a very different technology foundation,” said Rahul Regulapati, founder and CEO of Galleri5 and a partner at Collective Artists Network. “At Galleri5, we’re building that foundation with G5 AI Studio, bringing frontier AI models and filmmaking workflows into one platform. We’ve already demonstrated what this technology can do through films and television in India. Now, together with Indonesia’s extraordinary creative talent and Collective’s studio capabilities, we have an opportunity to take locally rooted stories to audiences around the world.” For Indonesian creators, the partnership is a chance to match stories led by local talent, and their own original IP, with tools meant to scale up production. Airlangga Hartarto, Indonesia’s coordinating minister for economic affairs and chairman of the National Council for Special Economic Zones, said the country had no plans to sit on the sidelines of AI development or simply act as a consumer of the technology. “We intend to help shape it. Special Economic Zones allow us to turn that ambition into real productivity, skilled jobs for our young people and new sources of growth on the path to 8 percent,” he said. Singhasari will introduce the venture to Indonesian creators, studios, investors, distributors and creative-economy institutions, and help set up local partnerships and routes to market. KRAT David Santoso KR, CEO of Lokanima and Singhasari Special Economic Zone, said the Kingdom of Singhasari had flourished eight centuries ago on the land the zone now occupies. It was a hub for engineering, the arts, scholarship and government, and its culture was enriched by hundreds of years of contact with India. “Today, with our partners from India, we are bringing that history back to life, this time by mastering the AI transformation. Our aim is to build new competitiveness for Indonesia in the new-technology and digital-content subsectors, with Indonesian talent and IP at its heart,” he said. India’s ambassador to Indonesia, Sandeep Chakravorty, said the Ramayana and the Mahabharata had been part of Indonesian temple culture, wayang (traditional puppet theater) and the popular imagination for over a millennium. “Today, India and Indonesia are writing the next chapter of that shared story with artificial intelligence,” he said. title: Anthropic Sued for Using Elvis Presley Music to Train AI Models
full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All October 24, 2026 7:22pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'EPiC: Elvis Presley in Concert' Courtesy of EPiC: Elvis Presley in Concert Anthropic has been sued by the owners of Elvis Presley ‘s music for allegedly utilizing his songs to train AI models without permission. As reported by Billboard , the suit was filed Friday and claims the company infringed 274 songs of Presley’s, including “Can’t Help Falling in Love,” “A Little Less Conversation” and “Don’t Be Cruel.” “The Elvis Plaintiffs bring this action to enforce these exclusive rights against the defendant that has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before,” wrote lead attorney Richard Busch. “The Elvis Plaintiffs are deeply protective of these iconic songs.” Related Stories Music Chappell Roan Enlists PinkPantheress to Close Out Super Graphic Spectacular Fundraising Shows General News Teen Study: YouTube Rules, AI Doom Increases With Age and Moviegoing Beats Sports on Weekends Authentic Brands Group, which owns the rights to Presley , filed the lawsuit alongside other entities that also own rights to the “Jailhouse Rock” singer, according to Billboard . “‘Claude’ has created infringing output of copyrighted material of virtually every song from every catalog available on the internet, including the Works,” the lawsuit states, per Rolling Stone . “Even after the Defendant supposedly put up ‘guardrails’ after being sued, in one of its latest iterations, Claude continues to infringe: when recently asked to recreate specific songs ‘for a modern audience,’ Claude did so and admitted: ‘These renders keep landing very close to the originals: same structure, same hooks reused with light rewording, and full sets of verses/choruses/bridges. That’s edging past ‘inspired by’ into reproducing the copyrighted song, even when the words are swapped out.’” In August, Round Hill sued Suno and Anthropic , claiming mass copyright infringement. They alleged the AI companies used hundreds of the publisher’s songs to train their AI models without permission. Anthropic was also previously sued by Universal Music Publishing, Abcko, Concord and BMG for similar claims of lyrics being utilized to train Claude, an AI agent. Rolling Stone reports that the suit is seeking $150,000 per infringed song. The Hollywood Reporter reached out to Anthropic for comment, but did not hear back. THR

Stallone famously sold Butkus for $40 when before he found fame because he couldn’t afford to feed him. After selling the “Rocky” script, he bought him back for $15,000. title: Nathan Fielder Negotiated a ‘Kill Switch’ on ‘You Can See Everything,’ Says Lance Oppenheim: ‘If We Didn’t Find Something, We Could Just Throw It All Away’
full_text: Oct 24, 2026 5:01pm PT Nathan Fielder Negotiated a ‘Kill Switch’ on ‘You Can See Everything,’ Says Lance Oppenheim: ‘If We Didn’t Find Something, We Could Just Throw It All Away’ By Zack Sharf , Payton Turkeltaub Add us as a Google Preferred Source A24 “ You Can See Everything ” might be the buzziest film of the moment, but before the Elizabeth Holmes-focused documentary made it to theaters, co-director Lance Oppenheim has admitted that fellow director Nathan Fielder was so skeptical about being able to weave a unique enough narrative that he negotiated a “kill switch” with A24 before they began filming. In an interview with IndieWire , Oppenheim detailed Fielder’s kill-switch idea and how it helped the project. While Fielder wanted to pursue the documentary with Oppenheim, he worried that “the story had been told so many times already.” (Before the documentary even began production, Holmes’ scandal was already the subject of a popular podcast, best-selling book, an Alex Gibney doc and “The Dropout,” the Hulu scripted series.) title: Jeff Garlin Considered Suicide After Tumultuous ‘Goldbergs’ Exit
full_text: × Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All October 24, 2026 2:11pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jeff Garlin at the 17th annual Thirst Gala in L.A. this past May. Gonzalo Marroquin/Getty Images for Thirst Project After Jeff Garlin left the ABC comedy The Goldbergs following an HR investigation stemming from multiple complaints about his behavior, he struggled mentally to the point that he considered ending his life. “I had a nervous breakdown, and I was going to commit suicide,” the actor said this week on Ted Danson ‘s Where Everybody Knows Your Name podcast. Garlin contacted his and Danson’s fellow Curb Your Enthusiasm co-star Susie Essman , who got Garlin’s friends to help him get treatment. Related Stories TV Where to Watch 'Grey's Anatomy' Season 23 Online TV Val Chmerkovskiy Returns to 'Dancing With the Stars' After One-Episode Suspension “I reached out to Susie [Essman], and I said, ‘I hate when people don’t reach out, but at noon today I will be dead. I’m letting you know I will be dead.’,” the actor recalled. “And she called [ex-wife] Marla, and she called [girlfriend] Sari and my friend, Brad Morris,” he said. “My girlfriend and my ex-wife called him. He’s one of my best friends. He watched me while they were looking for a place for me to go.” Ultimately Garlin checked into rehab in Cincinnati, Ohio, and underwent dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), which helped him overcome his suicidal thoughts. “I was no longer suicidal,” he said. “They helped get me to a point where I could stand, and then I went out in the world and it took time between therapy and medication for bipolar all that stuff to where I felt kind of whole.” In 2022, Garlin revealed he was bipolar, recently claiming the undiagnosed mental health condition affected his behavior on The Goldbergs . Garlin said he’s “now feeling really good” and is “very content,” adding that he’s sharing his mental health struggles to raise awareness. “The point is … for people who do what we do, we get just as dark as you do,” he said. “We have bad days just like you do. And I, Jeff Garlin, comedian, joyful gentleman, was going to end his life. But I’m grateful that I had friends and family. And then people have been so supportive of me.” Garlin left The Goldbergs in December 2021 after more than eight seasons playing father Murray Goldberg. The mutual decision between Garlin and production company Sony Pictures Television came during production on the ABC series’ ninth season and followed investigations from HR and Vanity Fair , with the latter reporting on an alleged pattern of verbal and physical conduct that made staffers uncomfortable. “My opinion is, I have my process about how I’m funny, in terms of the scene and what I have to do. They feel that it makes for a quote ‘unsafe’ workspace. Now, mind you, my silliness making an unsafe workspace — I don’t understand how that is. And I’m on a comedy show. I am always a kind and thoughtful person,” Garlin told Vanity Fair in December 2021. THR

title: Billy Corgan Defends Marilyn Manson Friendship Despite Sexual Assault Claims Against Manson: “I Didn’t Feel That He Was Guilty”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All October 24, 2026 11:44am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Marilyn Manson and Billy Corgan at a SiriusXM event in Chicago in 2015. Timothy Hiatt/Getty Images for SiriusXM Billy Corgan has defended his ongoing friendship with Marilyn Manson despite the latter being accused of sexual assault and abuse by multiple women. “As a Christian person, you have to stand by your friends, but that doesn’t mean you don’t have an opinion, and it doesn’t mean you’re not critical,” Corgan said on the New York Times ‘ Popcast earlier this week. “In his case — and I’m not here to adjudicate it — but the D.A. looked at the case for five years.” The Smashing Pumpkins frontman added: “In some cases, I knew personal things behind the scenes that are not in the public sphere. I personally didn’t feel that he was guilty of the things that he was being charged with, and ultimately the fact that the DA didn’t pursue … [it] was commensurate with the person I knew.” Related Stories Movies Joey King Reveals Conversation With Evan Rachel Wood After Replacing Her in 'Practical Magic 2' TV 'The Shards' Review: Ryan Murphy and Bret Easton Ellis Team Up for FX's Predictably Excess-Soaked Tale of Prep-School Sex, Drugs and Murder Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman announced in January 2025 , after investigating for four years, that his office wouldn’t pursue criminal charges against Manson, whose real name is Brian Warner, saying the statute of limitations had run out on the domestic violence claims against him and that prosecutors couldn’t prove charges of sexual assault beyond a reasonable doubt. “We recognize and applaud the courage and resilience of the women who came forward to make reports and share their experiences, and we thank them for their cooperation and patience with the investigation,” Hochman’s office said in a statement at the time. “While we are unable to bring charges in this matter, we recognize that the strong advocacy of the women involved has helped bring greater awareness to the challenges faced by survivors of domestic abuse and sexual assault.” Manson has faced accusations of sexual misconduct from numerous women, including actresses Evan Rachel Wood and Esmé Bianco as well as model Ashley Morgan Smithline and former assistant Ashley Walters. Wood, who was in a relationship with Manson for a number of years, came forward with her claims in 2021. “The name of my abuser is Brian Warner, also known to the world as Marilyn Manson,” she alleged on Instagram at the time. “He started grooming me when I was a teenager and horrifically abused me for years. I was brainwashed and manipulated into submission. I am done living in fear of retaliation, slander or blackmail.” Manson sued Wood for defamation in 2022 but he dropped the lawsuit in 2024 , and the two reached a settlement in which he agreed to cover her legal fees. Manson, who has denied all of the allegations against him, has faced civil lawsuits from Bianco, settling her case in 2023 ; Smithline, whose case was dismissed that year, and she later recanted her claims ; and Walters, whose sexual abuse lawsuit was recently reopened for a second time . “I guess it’s one of those things where I don’t want the world to tell me who my friends are and who I should associate with,” Corgan told Popcast . “That’s politically, socially, and in Brian’s case, we have a relationship that goes back close to 30 years.” Corgan also noted that Manson’s wife Lindsay’s twin sister is married to the Pumpkins’ James Iha, leading him to consider Manson “basically a part of our family.” “There’s a deeper set of relationships there,” he added. Beyond that, Corgan hinted at some insider knowledge of the legal proceedings against Manson that allowed him to make the determinations he did. “Anyone in that situation struggles with the accusations, the seriousness of the accusations. But again, I also knew the inside baseball of the case. I knew certain people who were involved, and so you make those evaluations,” Corgan said. “At the end of the day, I feel I made the right determination, but if things had come out….” he said. “Like people would ask me privately, ‘Well what happens if da da da…’ And I’d say, ‘If he’s guilty or anybody in that situation is guilty, they should go to jail.’ I’m not saying I have any moral supremacy here. I’m saying it’s a case-by-case basis. But I don’t like the idea of… this kind of witch mob thing bothers me.” THR

title: Jay-Z’s Victory Lap Continues as He Brings Out Blue Ivy Carter, John Legend, DJ Khaled for SoFi Stadium Opening Night

The rap icon was met with cheers as he, at last, brought his yearlong victory tour to Los Angeles. Indeed, it’s been close to a decade since Jay last played a full-fledged solo concert in the city, with Shawn Carter closing out his 4:44 Tour across the street at the Forum in 2017 and playing the Rose Bowl for his joint On the Run Tour with Beyoncé a year later. After a historic three-night run in New York at Yankee Stadium and a few more shows in London and Paris, not to mention an eight-part HBO docuseries directed by Rick Rubin, it’s finally L.A.’s turn, as Jay kicked off the first of two much-anticipated concerts Friday night in celebration of the 30th anniversary of his debut album Reasonable Doubt and 25th anniversary of The Blueprint. Kicking off just before 9:30 p.m. local time, the show opened with a video of Jay and Beyoncé alone in the seats at Yankee Stadium, with Bey behind him playing with her husband’s hair. Flanked by an impressive backing band and starting the night with “Hovi Baby,” Jay powered through a collection of hits and fan favorites for two hours, from “FuckWithMeYouKnowIGotIt” to “Run This Town,” “Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem),” “Lucifer” and “99 Problems.” “Let me take you back to my home for a second,” Jay told the crowd before launching into “Empire State of Mind” toward the end of the evening. title: Online Comedians Are Making a Mint Mocking Wall Street
full_text: × Skip to main content By Andrew Zucker Plus Icon Andrew Zucker View All October 24, 2026 10:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Screenshot/YouTube Johnny Hilbrant Partridge never worked an hour on Wall Street, but you’d never guess that by looking at him. Nearly every day, Partridge takes to YouTube to channel his inner finance bro as P.E. Guy, a puffer-vested private equity putz who brags about his million-dollar deals, Aspen manse and private plane. Partridge, who once taught fitness classes in Boston, debuted the character on social media last year, which boosted his following beyond Barry’s and SoulCycle devotees. Today, he has 400,000-plus Instagram followers, up from 7,000 about 18 months ago. Related Stories Influence Peddlers Top Creators' Secret Weapon? Indian Video Editors Music Anthropic Sued for Using Elvis Presley Music to Train AI Models Although Partridge lampoons private equity, his skits resonate beyond buyout boys. “I think a lot of people have that experience of coming in contact with somebody who wants to one-up you and make you feel like they win the conversation because they have an impressive-sounding job,” he says. As certain business figures become as talked about as celebrities, Wall Street yuksters like Partridge are surging on social media. While memes still flood finance bro DMs, creator-helmed videos are gaining momentum on both Wall Street and Main Street. Some riff on Bloomberg headlines, while others simply play on C-suite stereotypes. Other creators skewering corporate life include The Swiss Chris (442,000 Instagram followers), who portrays a highfalutin European banker; Clemente Varas Collado (115,000 Instagram followers), who frequently roasts asset manager BlackRock, and engineer-turned-entertainer Varun Rana (90,000 Instagram followers). It’s not an entirely new trend — Wall Street meme pages have been around for over a decade — but social media algorithms are increasingly favoring shortform video, benefiting creator-actors over anonymous meme lords. It’s led to stalling growth for some picture-heavy accounts, including Trust Fund Terry, which launched about eight years ago on Instagram. Trust Fund Terry has never revealed his identity, though he admits on the phone that he has toiled in consulting and finance. Terry, a pseudonym, said audience building on Instagram has become more difficult thanks to Reels. “I think they’ve really been trying to push the more traditional creators, where they’re telling a story in either short or longform video,” he said. Varun Rana. Courtesy Of Subject The Swiss Chris, who shows his face but remains anonymous, says he first played a character named Goldman Stanley. Chris, who was a banker in Europe, says the industry is one “where the humor practically writes itself.” Josh Kaplan, who runs creator management company Smooth Media, says part of these creators’ success is making their followers feel like they’re alongside Blackstone associates at the watercooler. “I feel like people love being on like the inside of a joke,” says Kaplan, whose company manages Rana. Josh Brown, the CNBC fixture and CEO of Ritholtz Wealth Management, is in numerous texting chains with Wall Streeters who pass around Partridge’s latest videos. He says Partridge’s P.E. Guy character is identifiable to the finance crowd. “When I first started my career in the late ’90s, it was investment bankers who were doing all the IPOs,” he says. “Now in the 2020s, the personification of that level of douchiness is private equity.” These Wall Street jesters are ascending at a moment when there’s immense interest in the machinations of finance firms and rainmakers. Some of the biggest sports storylines now involve the corporate dealings of billionaire owners. Hollywood A-listers are romancing private equity guys. And many consumers are keenly aware of investors behind businesses. P.E. Guy, aka Johnny Hilbrant Partridge (who uses a filter to create his character’s grotesque face.) Pat Greenhouse/The Boston Globe via Getty Images Brown believes Partridge’s and other creators’ outrageous personas stem from the growing number of people with equally outrageous wealth. “It’s a level of satire that television really hasn’t caught up to,” he says. “I think these people are nailing it in a way that maybe 20 years ago The Simpsons would have.” P.E. Guy still attracts the real-life P.E. guys, especially on LinkedIn, where he has over 10 times more followers than on X. “I’ve been able to satirize stuff on LinkedIn in a really fun way, where people don’t always know that it’s a joke because of how absurd things already are on LinkedIn,” he says, “which really tickles me.” This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: AMC Theatres Wants NYC’s Endangered Kips Bay Multiplex To Remain But Decision “Not Ours To Make”; Scheduled Closing Date Announced

title: Lowden, Turner or a Dark Horse: One James Bond Casting Test Has Nothing to Do With Acting
full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All October 24, 2026 9:48am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Pierce Brosnan in 1995's 'Goldeneye.' United Artists/courtesy Everett Collection Logo text Final James Bond screen tests have begun, which means there’s a chance that while you’re reading this an actor is auditioning in London for the biggest role of their life, a casting that could make its mark on one of the world’s longest-running film franchises. The oddsmakers — taking a cue from The Hollywood Reporter and others’ reporting — suggest Jack Lowden and Callum Turner are the favorites . Both have their apparent pros and cons. Lowden has a very likable presence on Apple TV’s Slow Horses , where he plays MI5 agent River Cartwright. For years, the role has looked like an audition for Bond. All the things Bond does — drama, action, romance, stunts — are on display, even though Lowden’s character has a rather different low-key vibe than 007. He’s an everyman pick, and that’s a rather refreshing idea that would give Bond writers new notes to explore with the character. Related Stories General News Hannah Einbinder Says Speaking Out for Palestine Is "the Bare Minimum" Movies Jack Lowden, Margaret Qualley Top Bookie Odds for Next James Bond and Bond Girl Turner looks like he might have been grown in a lab to play Bond, which is the best thing about him as a choice, but also a potential detriment if producers want somebody who feels more original. He seems could be perfect for the part — handsome and suave and posh. Between him and Lowden, Turner would also likely win the sex appeal contest. Reportedly in the mix are Jack O’Connell and Josh O’Connor — two actors with such similar names one wonders if sources leaking to the press got the two mixed up and only one of them is actually auditioning. Regardless of who gets the part, there is a lot more to playing Bond than merely fighting and bantering and firing a Walther PPK. There are qualities that many pundits on the sidelines might overlook, but Bond’s producers most assuredly will not: Bond may be a rogue character who plays by his own rules, but the actor cast in the role has to be the ultimate team player. Bond is a massive commitment that requires an actor to adhere to the highest professional standards for more than a decade. The actor may not always be playing Bond, but will forever be a Bond, and therefore must be counted upon to not embarrass the franchise. This means the choice should be somebody who, for instance, isn’t going to sound off divisively about politics, get into messy domestic disputes or start going on public benders. More subtly, it means somebody who’s down to be an agreeable brand ambassador for the part, who will treat fans respectfully and gamely participate in the intense media circus which accompanies every Bond film. They also have to, preferably, not be a jerk behind the scenes — missing on that one could make the typical nine-month production process for a Bond film much more difficult for all involved. These things are true for any lead role in a movie, but they’re far more true for playing Bond due to the iconic importance of the character and expected four-or-five-film commitment. The last thing Team Bond wants is a scandal like the one that befell Marvel after casting Jonathan Majors in a multi-film villain role. That was a mess , and resulted in an announced movie being scrapped. Yet Majors’ part was merely a villain amid an ensemble cast, not a lead who’s on camera in just about every scene. Legendary Bond producer Cubby Broccoli once said casting George Lazenby for 1969’s On Her Majesty’s Secret Service was “biggest mistake in 16 years.” Broccoli said the actor “just couldn’t deal with success. He was so arrogant.” Lazenby made just one Bond film before Sean Connery returned to the role. While Broccoli’s daughter, Barbara, who led the producing team on Bond until just last year, noted to Variety in 2022, “When we cast Bond, it’s a 10-, 12-year commitment … Not everybody wants to do that … It’s not just showing up for a couple of months of filming.” THR

full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All October 24, 2026 8:56am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'You Can See Everything' A24 Logo text Clayface rolls into the box office fray but faces competition from the second weekend of You Can See Everything as the buzzy Elizabeth Holmes documentary expands. Warner Bros. released director James Watkins’ body-horror feature Clayface in more than 3,400 North American theaters and it grossed $10.4 million domestically on Friday, including Thursday previews , adding $4.3 million internationally for the day. Earning an A- CinemaScore from audiences, Clayface could be headed for around $24 million domestically for the weekend, which would be just under the studio’s initial projection of $25 million to $30 million. Related Stories Movies 'Street Fighter' Breakout Callina Liang Talks Embracing Fan Skepticism and Reveals Two Key Scrapped Moments Movies 'Clayface' Soaks Up $3.5M in Box Office Previews as 'You Can See Everything' Expands This marks the first DC Studios movie to launch since Supergirl had a disappointing opening of $37.1 million domestically over the summer on a $170 million budget. The $44 million-budgeted Clayface has impressed critics more than Supergirl , with a 76 score from reviewers on Rotten Tomatoes and a 94 from audiences. In his r e view for The Hollywood Reporter , critic Frank Scheck called Clayface “a big swing that definitely pays off.” Tom Rhys Harries and Naomi Ackie star in the story of Matt Hagen (Harries), an actor who turns to a scientist (Ackie) for assistance when his face becomes disfigured. You Can See Everything collected $6.1 million on Friday from 2,600 North American locations to bring its domestic cume to $31.7 million. The A24 film, which has been building awards buzz , adds to last weekend’s momentum and could collect $20 million in its sophomore frame. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim ‘s documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Holmes widened after opening with $15 million from 855 theaters domestically, which gave it the highest-grossing launch for a release under 1,000 theaters since 2006’s Borat . Naomi Ackie (left) and Tom Rhys Harries in Clayface. Courtesy Warner Bros. Pictures Looking to take third place is Laika’s stop-motion animated movie Wildwood , grossing $4.2 million Friday and heading to an expected $11.2 million for the weekend. Carey Mulligan, Peyton Elizabeth Lee and Jacob Tremblay lead the voice cast for Travis Knight’s feature about a teen girl venturing to an enchanted forest to save her baby brother. Earning an A CinemaScore, Wildwood holds a dazzling 100 percent approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with Scheck heralding it as “ stupendous in every aspect .” After winning the box office battle last weekend, Paramount and Legendary’s Street Fighter looks to land around $8.4 million with a roughly 73 percent decline to move its domestic cume to $46.7 million. Noah Centineo, Andrew Koji and Callina Liang lead director Kitao Sakurai’s adaptation of the Capcom video game centering on a combat tournament. Wildwood Courtesy of Laika Likely to round out the top five is Black Bear’s romantic fantasy Wicker , which picked up $2.3 million domestically on Friday, including Thursday previews, from 1,471 North American theaters and is expected to open with $5.5 million. Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgard star in directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer’s movie about a woman in a quiet village who gets a wicker husband. In his review for THR , critic Richard Lawson praised Wicker’ s “winning mix of irreverence and compassion.” It holds a 94 score on Rotten Tomatoes from both critics and audiences. Opening quietly in 880 North American theaters from Sony Pictures is Taika Waititi ‘s Klara and the Sun , which made $300,000 and heads to around $725,000 for the weekend. Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams lead the adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel about a robot companion connecting with a sick girl. THR chief film critic David Rooney deemed it a “ wretched mess .” Additionally, Amazon MGM Studios releases Sacha Baron Cohen’s Ali G: Who Iz I? in just 125 theaters on only Friday and Saturday ahead of its Prime Video debut. full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Karoline Leavitt Compares Katie Zacharia’s Abrupt Exit As Trump’s Press Secretary To ‘The Apprentice’: “He’s Known For … Moving On From People” FCC’s Sole Democrat Calls On Broadcast Lobby To Push Back On Trump-Backed Chairman’s Regulatory Threats Over Election Coverage Donald Trump Lashes Out At NBC News Reporter As She Presses Him On Why He Supports Ad That Has Been Condemned By Democrats And Republicans View All October 1, 2026 3:02pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Chris Harrison’s The Vow' Fox Nation Fox News Media is rejecting Warner Bros’ claim that the upcoming Fox Nation reality series Chris Harrison ‘s The Vow infringes on its copyright and trademarks to The Bachelor . The new dating series, set to debut in November, is hosted by Harrison, who hosted The Bachelor from 2002-2021. Related Stories News Chris Harrison’s Dating Series ‘The Vow’ Sets Premiere On Fox Nation News Chris Harrison Calls His Exit From ‘The Bachelor’ Franchise “A Very Toxic Situation”: I’m “Grateful That I’m Gone” In a cease-and-desist letter reviewed by Deadline, Ahassim Rashid, VP and intellectual property counsel for Warner Bros Entertainment, owner of The Bachelor , claimed that the teaser for The Vow contained unauthorized uses of the studio’s IP. The attorney cited images of red rose petals “falling in the background with text in the foreground,” and noted that WB had licensed that motif to third parties for separate advertisements and promotion. The attorney also objected to the use of the words “The Bachelor” in the teaser, followed by the image of a man in a tux holding a rose. Also cited was the image of a “mansion in the background meant to evoke the iconic ‘Bachelor Mansion.'” Watch on Deadline Rashid wrote that the teaser “represents a plain attempt to capitalize on and ‘ride on the coattails'” of The Bachelor. In reply, Fox News Media ‘s executive VP and general counsel Katherine Moran Meeks contended that Warner Bros’ attorneys “wrongly assume that Warner Bros. holds any intellectual property rights whatsoever in a falling roses motif or in the words ‘The Bachelor’ when used colloquially to describe a single man.” In the Warner Bros letter, its attorney wrote that they have “no objection” to Fox and Lionsgate “releasing a dating show hosted by Chris Harrison in and of itself.” But Moran Meeks also claimed that Warner Bros was targeting Harrison in “this malicious and vindictive manner.” Fox News Media argued that the use of the falling rose petals are scènes à faire, or “stock elements long associated with the romance genre that have featured in films from American Beauty to Moulin Rouge to Beauty and the Beast . The network also contended that the use of the words “The Bachelor” is protected speech. “Even assuming this fleeting use of ‘The Bachelor’ is also a tongue-in-cheek reference to your show, that kind of ‘word-play, ambiguity, irony and allusion’ receives full protection of the First Amendment and cannot support a claim for trademark infringement,” Moran Meeks wrote. Warner Bros. has yet to comment further. The Hollywood Reporter first reported on the tussle over the new show.
